Most Peyronie's disease sufferers can still engage in sexual activity. Nonetheless, it can be painful and lead to erectile dysfunction in some people.
You may choose observation, medicinal, or surgical therapies depending on the symptoms.

Physicians are unsure of the precise cause of Peyronie's illness. Numerous researchers think that trauma (striking or bending) that results in internal bleeding in the penis can induce the fibrous plaque to develop. You might not be aware of the trauma or injury.
Genes may also play a role in other conditions that progress over time. In certain guys, both genetics and injuries may be at play.

It's possible for symptoms to occur suddenly or gradually. If the penis is soft, no issue is visible. Yet, in extreme situations, the hardened plaque restricts flexibility, hurting and causing the penis to arc or bend when upright.
The pain typically subsides with time, but the penis bent may get worse.

Other parts of the body, such the hand or foot, may also develop scar tissue in some individuals with the illness. Peyronie's disease appears to be more common in men who have Dupuytren's contractures, a scarring condition that affects the fingers of the hand.

faqs.q: Can Viagra fix Peyronie's?
faqs.a: No, Viagra does not fix peyronie’s disease. But, it can help with erectile dysfunction which is one of the symptoms of peyronie’s disease.

faqs.q: Can Peyronie's be temporary?
faqs.a: Yes, peyronie’s disease goes away on its own in most cases in 6-15 months. In mild cases, it will go away on its own and in some severe cases it may become permanent.

faqs.q: How painful is Peyronie's surgery?
faqs.a: There may be mild pain and burning sensation after surgery. Also, you can overcome this mild pain using antibiotics like acetaminophen. In most cases, pain will go away in one week after surgery.

faqs.q: Can Peyronie's come back after surgery?
faqs.a: Yes, peyronie’s disease has chances of coming back after surgery. To avoid a second surgery you can wait until the symptoms get worse to treat your first surgery.

blocks.text: Ejaculatory Disorder refers to a condition where a person has difficulty ejaculating or reaching orgasm during sexual activity. There are different types of ejaculatory disorders, including premature ejaculation, delayed ejaculation, and retrograde ejaculation. Premature ejaculation is when a person ejaculates too quickly, often within one minute of sexual activity.

Delayed ejaculation is when a person has difficulty ejaculating or cannot ejaculate at all, even with prolonged sexual stimulation. Retrograde ejaculation occurs when sperm enters the bladder rather than departing the body via the penis during ejaculation. Ejaculatory disorders can be caused by various factors, including psychological issues, medications, nerve damage, and hormonal imbalances. Treatment methods may include counseling, medication, or a change in lifestyle.
The treatment for ejaculatory disorder depends on the type and underlying cause of the condition. Here are some common treatment options:

items: Behavioral techniques: Behavioral techniques such as the squeeze technique and start-stop technique can help with premature ejaculation. These techniques involve stopping sexual stimulation before ejaculation and using certain physical or mental techniques to delay ejaculation.
Medications: Certain medications such as antidepressants, topical anesthetics, and phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitors (PDE5 inhibitors) can be used to treat premature ejaculation or delayed ejaculation.
Hormone therapy: Hormone therapy may treat ejaculatory disorders caused by hormonal imbalances.
Psychological counseling: Counseling or therapy may be helpful for ejaculatory disorders caused by psychological issues such as anxiety, depression, or relationship problems.

Surgery: In rare cases, surgery may be recommended for retrograde ejaculation caused by nerve damage or other structural issues. It is important to consult a healthcare professional for proper diagnosis and treatment of ejaculatory disorders.

faqs.q: What is the treatment for ejaculatory dysfunction?
faqs.a: Treatment varies based on the type of dysfunction. Options include selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) for premature ejaculation, while delayed ejaculation may be treated with medications like bupropion or counseling for psychological issues.

faqs.q: How to avoid quick discharge of sperm?
faqs.a: To manage premature ejaculation, techniques such as behavioral therapy, pelvic floor exercises, and medications like SSRIs can be effective. Additionally, using desensitizing creams or condoms may help prolong the duration before ejaculation.

faqs.q: How to stop pre-ejaculatory fluid?
faqs.a: While pre-ejaculatory fluid is a natural response, if it's excessive, techniques like pelvic floor exercises or behavioral methods can help manage it. Consulting a healthcare provider may also provide personalized strategies.

faqs.q: How can I increase my ejaculatory control?
faqs.a: Improving ejaculatory control can involve practicing techniques such as the "stop-start" method, engaging in pelvic floor exercises, and possibly using medications prescribed by a healthcare professional. Counseling may also address underlying psychological factors.
